description: Reducing average voyage speed by 1 to 2 knots significantly lowers fuel consumption and CO₂ emissions due to the cubic relationship between speed and power.
sources: Faber, J. et al. (2020). Fourth IMO GHG Study 2020. IMO.
Cariou, P. (2011). Is slow steaming a sustainable means of reducing CO₂ emissions from container shipping? Transportation Research Part D, 16(3), 260-264.

description: Optimising voyage routes to minimise distance and adverse weather, combined with hull trim adjustments, reduces drag and fuel consumption.
sources: Psaraftis, H.N. & Kontovas, C.A. (2013). Speed models for energy-efficient maritime transportation. Transportation Research Part C, 26, 331-351.

description: Using meteorological data to plan routes that avoid heavy weather, minimising added resistance and fuel consumption.
sources: Shao, W. et al. (2018). Development of a novel forward dynamic programming method for weather routing. Ocean Engineering, 150, 240-250.

description: Regular removal of biofouling from hull and propeller surfaces restores hydrodynamic efficiency and reduces fuel penalty from increased roughness.
sources: Adland, R. et al. (2018). The value of meteorological data in marine risk assessment. Reliability Engineering & System Safety, 169, 58-68.

description: Application of advanced anti-fouling and friction-reducing coatings during drydocking to reduce hull drag and fuel consumption over the coating lifecycle.
sources: Lindgren, J.F. et al. (2016). Fuel efficiency and exhaust emissions. In Shipping and the Environment, Springer, 1-27.

description: Installation of devices such as pre-swirl stators, Mewis ducts, or propeller boss cap fins to improve propulsive efficiency.
sources: Mäkiharju, S.A. et al. (2012). On the energy economics of air lubrication drag reduction. International Journal of Naval Architecture and Ocean Engineering, 4(4), 412-422.

description: Capturing waste heat from engine exhaust to generate additional electrical power, reducing auxiliary engine load and overall fuel consumption.
sources: Shu, G. et al. (2013). A review of waste heat recovery on two-stroke IC engine aboard ships. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, 19, 385-401.

measure: Biofuel blending (e.g., POME B10 to B20)
description: Blending palm oil methyl ester (POME) or other biodiesel with conventional marine fuel. Combustion-level research has validated NOx and CO₂ reduction potential at the engine scale.
sources: Wan Mansor, W.N. et al. (2022). The NOx Reduction Performances for Blended Palm Oil Methyl Ester in Marine Diesel Engine.

description: Operating engines in dual-fuel mode with LNG as primary fuel reduces CO₂ and virtually eliminates SOx and PM. Computational modelling has validated the combustion dynamics and emission profiles.
sources: Wan Mansor, W.N. et al. (2016). Computational Modeling of Diesel and Dual Fuel Combustion.
Wan Mansor, W.N. et al. (2015). Effects of Diesel Displacement on the Emissions.
Balcombe, P. et al. (2019). How to decarbonise international shipping. Energy Conversion and Management, 182, 72-88.

description: Complete transition to LNG as primary fuel for new builds or major retrofits. Offers significant CO₂ reduction compared to HFO/MDO, though methane slip must be managed.
sources: Balcombe, P. et al. (2019). How to decarbonise international shipping. Energy Conversion and Management, 182, 72-88.
Pavlenko, N. et al. (2020). The climate implications of using LNG as a marine fuel. ICCT Working Paper.
